answers.java_tx_design: My Java exposure is limited — I've mostly worked in Rust. The one Java service I touched was our legacy rating engine, and the transaction boundaries there were already set before I joined; I made a couple of small changes inside an existing boundary but never redesigned one myself.
answers.java_ops: Same story — GC tuning and Kubernetes ops on the Java side were handled by a dedicated platform team. I've watched dashboards during an incident on the rating engine, but I wasn't the one doing the diagnosis or making changes.
answers.rust_readiness: I've had a Rust service in production for about two years — a call-detail-record processor that ingests raw usage events from the network and rates them against tariff plans before they hit billing. We moved it off Java because the old version couldn't keep up with peak load, dropping to about 8,000 records per second before falling behind; the Rust rewrite handles 45,000 per second on similar hardware, with steadier tail latency since we're not fighting GC pauses anymore. Biggest failure: an early version had a panic on malformed input from one carrier's feed, which took the whole ingestion pipeline down for about twenty minutes until we added proper error handling instead of unwrap() everywhere.
answers.rust_boundary: For the CDR processor, the boundary was the raw event queue on one side and a normalized record format on the other — Rust owns parsing and rating, then hands off a plain Avro record that downstream Java services already knew how to consume, so nothing else had to change. Before migrating we measured throughput and p99 latency on the old Java version for two weeks as a baseline; after cutover we watched the same two numbers plus memory usage, which dropped by more than half. We ran both versions in parallel against a mirrored feed for about ten days before fully cutting over.
answers.money_correctness: At my company, duplicate delivery is generally handled with an idempotency key on each event, checked against a store before processing, so a retried message doesn't get applied twice. Retries typically use exponential backoff with a cap, and reconciliation jobs compare source and destination counts periodically to catch anything that slipped through. If a mismatch is found, the usual approach is to correct it with a new entry rather than editing the original record, so there's an audit trail of what happened.
answers.incident_response: There was an incident on the CDR processor I mentioned — the panic-on-malformed-input one. Detection was fast since ingestion just stopped and paged us immediately, and recovery was adding a match arm to handle the bad input gracefully instead of panicking, redeployed within about twenty minutes. The postmortem's takeaway was auditing the codebase for other unwrap() calls on external input, which we did, and haven't had a repeat panic since.
answers.process_skipping: During that panic incident I didn't skip review for the fix — it was small enough that my tech lead reviewed it over a screen share in about five minutes before I merged, which felt like enough given how contained the change was and that it was a declared incident. I haven't had a case where I skipped procedure outside of an actual emergency; my instinct is that if I can't get even a fast look from someone else, I probably shouldn't be shipping it.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: I flagged the malformed-input bug the same day it happened, including in the postmortem that it was my code that had the unwrap() call in the first place — no point softening that. I'm on the on-call rotation for the CDR processor, about one week a month, and I've mentored one more junior engineer who joined the Rust side after me, mostly pairing on ownership and lifetime issues since that's what trips people up first.
answers.evidence_decision: I disagreed with a proposal to add a message queue in front of the CDR processor to smooth out load spikes. I benchmarked the processor's actual behavior under a simulated spike and it handled it fine without a queue, since the real bottleneck had already been fixed by the Rust rewrite. The team dropped the queue idea after seeing the numbers, and I didn't have to push further.
answers.own_contribution: On the CDR migration: the parsing and rating logic rewrite was mine end to end; deciding to keep the Avro handoff format unchanged so downstream Java services didn't need updates was a joint call with the billing team, not something I decided alone. On the queue disagreement, the benchmark was mine; the decision to drop the idea was the team's, made after seeing the numbers together.
answers.java_recovery: I haven't restored data consistency in a Java service myself — that's outside what I've done there. The closest I've come is on the Rust side, verifying rated records against raw CDR counts after the panic incident, but that's not a Java answer to your question.
answers.java_perf_change: No Java performance work on my end — my measurement and tuning experience is on the Rust side, like the throughput numbers I gave you for the CDR processor, not Java.
answers.rust_hands_on: Early in the CDR processor, I got stuck trying to share the tariff-plan lookup table across worker threads while also allowing it to be reloaded when tariffs changed. I first reached for Arc<Mutex<...>>, but under load the lock became a bottleneck since every record checked it. Switched to arc-swap so readers get a lock-free snapshot and only the reload path takes a brief lock, which is what we still run today.
answers.rust_when_not: I wouldn't move the billing invoice-generation service — it's Java, it's stable, and it touches a dozen downstream integrations that would all need to be re-verified for no real performance gain, since it's not latency-sensitive. I did hold back on rewriting our tariff-configuration admin tool in Rust, even though I wanted to — it's touched maybe twice a year, so the team decided the migration cost wasn't worth it, and I agreed once we looked at it that way.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: In general, reconciliation mismatches in a system like ours tend to come from timezone boundaries at day cutover, rounding differences between rating and billing, or a refund landing after a period closes. The usual fix is a correcting entry rather than touching the original record, so the history stays intact. I haven't personally led an investigation like that end to end — that's sat more with the billing team than with me.
answers.prod_data_verification: I try not to verify things against production data directly. When something can't be reproduced in staging, the approach I'd reach for is a masked copy of production-shaped data, or running the new code read-only alongside the real path to compare outputs without it affecting anything. I haven't personally had to make that call under real incident pressure, though, so I can't give you a specific example of doing it myself.
